ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Both studies were approved by the authors' Institutional Review Boards; Study 1 at New York University and Study 2 at the University of Amsterdam.
In each, all participants provided informed consent and received debriefing on the study's main purpose.
Participants US-based participants (N = 1,238) were recruited via the CloudResearch platform (Amazon MTurk) in the spring of 2022 and completed the study for $10.
All participants completed the study online.
After providing consent, participants completed a face annotation task unrelated to the present research.
Upon completion, participants were debriefed, thanked, and paid.
Participants US-based participants (N = 1,268) were recruited via the Prolific in the spring of 2026 and completed the study for $10.

Prolific's prescreening tool was used to limit participation to selfidentified White people living in the US and to include equal proportions of self-identified political liberals, moderates, and conservatives.
White-identified US-based participants (405 women, 496 men, 5 "other"; Mage = 40.46, range = 19-78; opt-in) were recruited via CloudResearch in spring 2022 and paid $10.
Study 206 White-identified US-based participants (585 women, 602 men, 19 "other"; Mage = 41.23, range = 18-84; opt-in) were recruited via Prolific in spring 2026 and paid $10.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Despite the popular narrative that White Americans supported Donald Trump in 2016 due to economic concerns, several studies show that their support is more strongly predicted by a variety of social issues concerning race and gender.

The present work sought to characterize the core features of these social issues among White Americans by assessing 15 self-report and behavioral measures of social attitudes, in addition to several economic, political, and demographic indicators, and comparing their relative effects on Trump support during the Biden and second Trump presidential terms.

In both studies, conducted in 2022 (N=906) and 2026 (N=1206), racial resentment was the strongest predictor of Trump support relative to all other measures of social, economic, and political concerns.
Economic stress was negatively associated with Trump support.
Furthermore, we find that, among conservatives, the relation between racial resentment and Trump support aligns more closely with MAGA identity than with conservatism generally.
These findings clarify the nature of White Americans' support for Trump, show its sustained association across presidential administrations, and link it closely to the MAGA movement.
What drives White Americans' support for Donald Trump?
Despite popular narratives invoking economic stress, several studies have shown that social issues regarding race and gender most strongly explain their support (1) (2) (3) (4).

text.text: However, the specific nature of these social issues and their effects relative to other political and economic factors remain unclear because these factors are rarely compared within a single investigation.

Furthermore, because most prior studies were conducted around the beginning of Trump's first term, immediately following the presidency of Barack Obama, the nation's first Black president, it is possible that the nature of White Americans' support for Trump has changed during the Biden administration and Trump's second term.
In the present work, we sought to characterize the social issues most strongly driving White Americans' Trump support and test whether these patterns have changed since Trump's first term.

White Americans' support for right-wing politicians has long been animated by anti-Black racial resentment (5, 6) and, indeed, this sentiment has been shown to predict their support for Trump in 2016 (4).

text.text: These findings-which implicate several distinct factors in White Americans' support of Trump-raise the question of whether these factors can be characterized by a dominant underlying motive or whether the specific social concerns of Trump supporters have changed over time.

text.text: To address these questions, we analyzed data from two large studies of White Americans with four major aims: To compare the effects of racial resentment and economic stress on Trump support, to characterize the type of social attitude that most strongly drives Trump support, to compare these social attitudes with popular alternative explanations, and to assess change in these patterns over the past four years.

Whereas nationally representative surveys (e.g., the American National Election Studies Survey) used in prior research have limited sets of very brief surveys, our research included an expanded set of measures, including behavioral assessments (e.g., of implicit prejudice) and multi-item questionnaires, while retaining gender balance, age variability, and representation across all 50 US states (see Methods and SI).
Study 1 (N=906, spring of 2022) assessed 15 measures of racial and gender-related attitudes and beliefs, as well as economic stress, ideology, and demographics (see SI).

Our focal measure of racial resentment was a six-item version of the Modern Racism Scale (6), which probes the denial of racial discrimination, resentment about diversity initiatives, and the belief that efforts to promote equality are unfair to White people.

text.text: Indeed, aside from a direct measure of ideology (see SI), racial resentment was the strongest unique predictor of all measured variables-even outpredicting right-wing authoritarianism and immigration attitudes in Study 2-suggesting that this construct captures a core concern driving White Americans' Trump support.

Our research further examined the extent to which this phenomenon-racial resentment driving White Americans' Trump support-reflects their broader conservative views or pertains more specifically to identification with the MAGA movement.

Study 2 found that while conservative and MAGA identities were highly overlapping among conservative participants, the link between racial resentment and Trump support was more characteristic of the MAGA movement than of conservatism at large.

In addition to these novel contributions, the results of both studies replicate prior findings associating racial issues, and not economic stress, with Trump support, suggesting again that popular narratives focused on economic issues may fail to capture the concerns leading White Americans to support Trump.

Together, these results reveal that social issues continue to predict White Americans' support for Donald Trump in 2022 and 2026, and that while these issues are multifaceted, the strongest unique predictor compared with all other examined social, economic, and demographic factors is anti-Black racial resentment.
